lead: A control survey fixes a small number of points to a much higher accuracy than the detail survey that follows. Horizontal control gives X and Y; vertical control gives Z. Everything else — a topographic sheet, a road centre line, a pipeline, a drone map — hangs on these points. An error in the detail stays local, but an error in control spreads into all later work. So control is observed first, checked, adjusted, and only then used as the frame for detail.
prereq: You need: Chapter 4.2 for horizontal and vertical angles, Chapter 4.5 for triangulation and trilateration, Unit 3 for differential levelling and booking, and Chapter 4.3 for trigonometric levelling.

sections.h3: Control is a sparse frame of known points

blocks.text: A control point is a point on the ground whose position is known to a stated accuracy and which is marked so that it can be found again. Its position is three numbers: X and Y in the chosen plane datum, and Z, the reduced level above the datum. A control network is a set of such points, tied together by observations and adjusted as one piece.

The detail survey that follows — compound walls, kerbs, trees, contours — is hung on the control. That is why control comes first. An error in a detail point stays at that one spot; an error in a control point is carried into every detail point fixed from it. Two parties working from the same control also join without a seam, which matters when a road surveyed by one consultant meets a drain surveyed by another.

Control is sparse on purpose: few points, each observed longer, with better instruments and repeated measurements. Density rises as the map gets finer. A 1:25 000 topo sheet can live with points a few kilometres apart; a layout plan for a housing colony needs points close enough to set out from, often a few hundred metres apart.

Control is graded by order. First order is the highest: tightest permitted misclosure, widest spacing. Second and third order fill in, and minor control is fixed from them for the detail survey. Some syllabi quote a permitted relative closing error of about 1 in 5000 for an ordinary minor traverse, and an order of magnitude tighter for first-order work.

sections.h3: Horizontal control: angles, sides or satellites

blocks.text: Horizontal control fixes X and Y. Four methods are in use.

items: Triangulation: one base line measured with great care, every other side computed from well-shaped observed angles (Chapter 4.5).
Trilateration: every side measured directly by EDM, angles optional.
Traverse: angles and sides measured along a route; suits corridors such as a road, a canal or a pipeline, where a chain of triangles is awkward.
GNSS: satellite ranges give X, Y and Z, and stations need not see each other; the standard choice for new work.

blocks.text: A control network is not trusted until it proves itself. The standard checks are: closing the horizon, where all angles around one station must sum to 360°; closing on a known point or a known side, where the computed value must match the fixed value within the permitted misclosure; a check base measured a second time by an independent method; and loop closure in a traverse, where the coordinates must return to the starting point. Traverse closing error and its adjustment are in Unit 2, and Chapter 4.7 shows how an accepted misclosure is distributed.

sections.h3: Vertical control, benchmarks and ground control points

blocks.text: Vertical control fixes Z. The instruments are the level and the staff, and the method is differential levelling (Unit 3). A run starts at a benchmark of known reduced level and closes back on it or on another benchmark. For a loop that returns to the same mark, the closing error is ΣBS − ΣFS, and the run is accepted only if it is within the permitted misclosure, written c√K mm, where K is the loop length in kilometres and c is a constant set by the order — about 4 for precise work, 12 for ordinary and 24 for rough.

Where the ground is too rough, or the point is a hilltop that cannot be reached, trigonometric levelling is used (Chapter 4.3). It is faster and works uphill, but it is weaker than a levelling run, so it serves lower-order vertical control or fills in between benchmarks.

A benchmark must be permanent and findable. A brass bolt in a culvert, a chisel mark on a gate pillar, a concrete block with a painted number: each needs a description — street or village, a sketch, and distances to two or three nearby objects. Without that record the mark is useless once the paint fades.

Ground control points (GCPs) are the same idea for photogrammetry, UAV flights and GIS base mapping: points with known X, Y and Z that show clearly in the imagery and georeference the whole block. Setting out hangs on the same frame — a building corner, a road chainage, a pipeline centre line is set out from control points, never from a nearby tree.

examples.question: A levelling loop starts at benchmark A with RL 250.000 m, runs 6 km, and closes back on A. The field book gives ΣBS = 12.824 m and ΣFS = 12.798 m. (a) Find the misclosure. (b) Decide whether to accept the run if the permitted misclosure is 12√K mm, with K in km. (c) State the correction per kilometre.
steps: For a loop that returns to its starting benchmark, the net rise must be zero. Net rise = ΣBS − ΣFS, where ΣBS is the sum of all backsights and ΣFS the sum of all foresights, both in metres.
Convert to millimetres: 0.026 × 1000 = 26 mm. The plus sign means the run finishes 26 mm high: the computed RL at A is 250.026 m against the known 250.000 m.
Permitted misclosure = 12√K mm, with K = 6 km: 12 × √6 = 12 × 2.4495 = 29.39 mm.
Compare: 26 mm < 29.39 mm, so the run is accepted.
Distribute the 26 mm with the opposite sign over the 6 km: 26 ÷ 6 = 4.33 mm per km, subtracted from the reduced level at each point in proportion to its distance along the run.
examples.answer: Misclosure +26 mm, permitted 29.39 mm, so the run is accepted; the 26 mm is distributed at 4.33 mm per km with the opposite sign.
examples.check:
import math
bs = 12.824
fs = 12.798
K = 6.0
mis_mm = (bs - fs) * 1000
perm = 12 * math.sqrt(K)
per_km = mis_mm / K
print(round(mis_mm, 2))
print(round(perm, 2))
print(round(per_km, 2))
print(mis_mm <= perm)

traps: Treating the detail survey as control. Control is observed first, to a tighter standard, and detail hangs on it; the reverse order cannot be repaired later.
Ignoring a misclosure that is inside the limit. It must be distributed, not dropped; a run outside the limit is repeated with better setups, not adjusted.
Sign slip in a closed loop: misclosure is ΣBS − ΣFS, so a positive value means the run finished high. The correction carries the opposite sign.
Unit slip in c√K mm: K must be in kilometres and the answer comes out in millimetres. Feeding K in metres inflates the limit by about 32 times.
Mixing up order and density. Higher order means a smaller permitted misclosure and fewer, more widely spaced points — not more points.

quiz.q: Define a control point and a control network.
quiz.a: A control point is a permanently marked ground point whose X, Y and Z are known to a stated accuracy. A control network is a set of such points observed together and adjusted as one frame.

quiz.q: Why is control observed before the detail survey?
quiz.a: Every detail point is fixed from control, so a control error is copied into all of them, while a detail error stays local. Control is also shared between parties, so both sets of detail join without a seam.

quiz.q: A loop of 9 km closes with ΣBS − ΣFS = −0.036 m. The permitted misclosure is 12√K mm. Is the run acceptable?
quiz.a: Misclosure = −36 mm. Permitted = 12√9 = 36 mm. The magnitude equals the limit, so the run is acceptable only at the limit; distribute the 36 mm with the opposite sign, here 4 mm per km added.

quiz.q: Why does a higher-order network allow a smaller permitted misclosure yet use wider spacing?
quiz.a: Higher order uses better instruments, longer observation periods and stronger geometry, so each point is far more accurate. Fewer such points are then enough, because the lower orders and the detail survey are fixed from them.

quiz.q: What is closing the horizon, and what does it detect?
quiz.a: It is the check that all horizontal angles measured around one station sum to 360°. A residual shows pointing or reading error, or a disturbed instrument.

quiz.q: Why are ground control points needed for a UAV survey if the drone carries GNSS?
quiz.a: On-board GNSS fixes the camera positions only to a few metres, and the block can drift. GCPs with known X, Y and Z pin the model to the ground datum and let the accuracy be checked at independent points.

beyond: Not for the exam. In practice, control networks are now usually observed with GNSS static sessions and processed against a national reference frame, with levelling used only where heights must be tight. Permanent marks are recorded in databases with photographs and coordinates, so the next surveyor can recover them years later. Continuous operating reference stations stream corrections, so a roving receiver gets centimetre positions in the field. Search for "GNSS continuously operating reference station", "network adjustment" and "ground control point accuracy standards" to go further.
